blocks.text: …full tuition at any university he chooses. And Mr. Hale has been trying to claim it for himself."
The audience murmured. Brandon went red and sat very still.
After the ceremony, the principal, Dr. Lorraine Mosley, introduced me to a man in a gray suit waiting by the stage. He was in his fifties, with a kind face I almost recognized.
"Mrs. Bennett," he said, using my maiden name. "You probably don't remember me. Marcus Hill. Fourth grade, 1982. I couldn't read."

I remembered. A small, angry boy who hid in the coat closet during reading time. His mother worked nights, and his father was gone. I kept him after school three days a week for a whole year and taught him to read with comic books, because that was what he'd agree to look at. By June, he was reading on grade level.
Marcus went on to build a software company in Atlanta and sell it for a great deal of money.

In 2004, he set up the Patricia Bennett Scholarship Fund at the school district where I taught, anonymously, because he didn't think I'd accept the attention. It had paid for college for more than two hundred students. He'd added one clause to the trust: any grandchild of mine who graduated from a school in the district would receive full tuition.

Brandon had found out about the fund last year from a school board member he golfed with. He'd been trying to get the trustees to pay Ethan's scholarship money directly to him, as Ethan's "financial guardian," with paperwork claiming I had died. The trustees grew suspicious and contacted Marcus. Marcus contacted Dr. Mosley. They'd decided to recognize me publicly at graduation so I'd finally know the truth, and so would everyone else.
The seventy-five-hundred-dollar "venue fee" Brandon charged me was money he'd collected from five relatives to cover debts.
The graduation, it turned out, was held in the school gym, free of charge.
My daughter, Rachel, didn't know any of it. She confronted Brandon in the parking lot. He returned every dollar to every relative within a week.
Ethan is at Vanderbilt now, studying education. He wants to teach fourth grade.

Marcus and I have lunch whenever he's in Nashville. Last time, he brought me a framed comic book, a worn copy of the first one he ever read all the way through. Inside the cover, in a child's handwriting from 1982, it says: "Mrs. Bennett says I'm smart."
